content.title: Artemis II latest: Moon mission astronauts receive heroes' welcome as they reunite with families following successful landing
content.text: GoodnightThat's all from today's live coverage of the latest on the Artemis II mission, thanks for following.After reuniting with their families, we heard from the four astronauts - Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen - for the first time this evening.You can watch some of their address to the world, live from Houston, Texas, here - and scroll through for even more of the highlights.The Artemis II crew's welcome back to EarthThe four Artemis II astronauts were reunited with their families today, before speaking publicly for the first time about their mission around the moon.Here are some more pictures from their welcome back to Earth.Beyond the moon: NASA's mission photosPhotos taken during the Artemis II mission were shared by NASA earlier today, following the crew's sucessful return.This first image shows an extraordinary view of the Earth peeking out over the horizon of the moon.This closer shot shows the craters dotting the surface.And here we can see Artemis II pilot Victor Glover taking in the view.'This is just the beginning - we're entering a new era of exploration'As the event finishes, the Artemis II crew get one final standing ovation and lots more cheers."This is just the beginning," the crowd is told. "We're entering a new era of exploration."Sky News' science and technology editor Tom Clarke, who is at the centre in Houston, says it was "quite remarkable" to see the astronauts on Earth, in person, following their historic 10-day mission."They showed so much humility," Clarke says of the crew. "I already thought they were heroes," he adds, but hearing them speak was "humbling".Artemis II was a test flight around the moon that went "almost flawlessly", he adds. The next missions include Artemis III and IV, which will go further and land on the moon.This is a huge moment for NASA and a celebration for all its astronauts, Clarke says, as well as all the scientists, engineers and mathematicians involved in the mission.'The world needed this,' congressman tells Artemis II crewTexas congressman Michael Cloud is now speaking on stage, and tells NASA's Johnson Space Center it is an honour to be there."Thank you for all you've done to inspire us," he tells the four Artemis II astronauts."Us as a nation desperately needed this, the world needed this..."You've inspired us and you've given us something we can build upon for the future."'There was a lot of joy up there'There are more hugs before Canadian astronaut and mission specialist Jeremy Hansen gets his turn.He says he wants to share the human experiences they had, starting with "gratitude" for his family, for NASA and the Canadian space agency, as well as the "bravery and courage" of everyone involved in the mission."There was a lot of joy up there," he continues, before joking that they were not always "on the joy train".He says he also wants to talk about "love"."When you look up here, you're not looking at us," he says. "We are a mirror reflecting you."There's another standing ovation for the astronauts as they hug it out.'Planet Earth - you are a crew'Pilot Victor Glover is now addressing the audience. "The gratitude of seeing what we saw, doing what we did and being who I was with, it's too big," he says."I wanted to thank our families," he adds, echoing words by Wiseman.There's another standing ovation and more hugs before mission specialist Christina Koch speaks."Ten days ago, this journey started with our mission manager knocking on my door," she says. "And it ended last night when my nurse on the ship put me to bed and said, 'Ma'am, can I get a hug?'"A lot has happened between those two moments but the start and the end were human events on Earth," she says.Koch then goes on to say that a crew is "a group that is in it, all the time, no matter what... that is willing to sacrifice silently for each other"."A crew has the same cares and the same needs," she adds. "A crew is inescapably, beautifully, dutifully linked."She says their impressions of "tiny Earth" wasn't just our planet, but "all the blackness around it". Earth was like a "lifeboat", she says, adding: "Planet Earth - you are a crew."'It's a special thing to be human and a special thing to be on planet Earth,' says Artemis II commanderWith their families seated in the audience, the four Artemis II astronauts are on stage in Houston.They received a standing ovation and cheers as they walked on, welcomed by NASA chief Jared Isaacman, who described Artemis II as the "opening act" for America's return to the moon."Thank you for contributing to the greatest adventure in human history," Isaacman told them.Commander Reid Wiseman started by telling the crowd: "I have no idea what to say."He then told his fellow astronauts they were "bonded" forever.No one on Earth will know what the four went through, he said. "This was no easy... when you're out there, you just want to get back to your families and friends."It's a special thing to be human and a special thing to be on planet Earth."The four then share a hug on stage.'Mission complete': Commander shares photo of reunion with daughtersWe're still waiting for the astronauts to take their seats at NASA's Johnson Space Center, in Houston, Texas.Before then, we can bring you this update from Commander Reid Wiseman, who shared this photo on Instagram just over 20 minutes ago."Mission complete," he wrote, alongside a picture of himself and his two daughters.All the astronauts were set to reunite with their families ahead of giving their first statements. Astronauts expected to speak live from Houston shortlyThe four Artemis II astronauts are getting ready to speak at NASA's Johnson Space Center, in Houston, Texas, following their record-breaking 10-day mission around the moon.Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen have travelled some 252,756 miles from Earth - further than anyone else in the history of space travel.During their last hour in space, the crew passed over the southwestern coast of Australia."I think we see a beautiful sunrise," Wiseman told mission control.We are expecting to hear from them shortly, for the first time since their safe return to Earth.Moon mission astronauts arrive in Texas after successful return to EarthGood evening and welcome back to our live coverage of the Artemis II mission around the moon.We're picking back up following the astronauts' successful return to Earth in the early hours of this morning UK time, when the three Americans and one Canadian made a dramatic splashdown in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California.After almost 10 days in space, the NASA crew - commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen - were taken by helicopter to a nearby US Navy amphibious transport vessel, the John P Murtha, for medical examination.They have now arrived in Houston, Texas, to be reunited with their families - and are soon expected to make their first statements since returning to Earth.Stay with us for all the latest updates.We're pausing our live coverage - but we'll be back soonThanks for following our live coverage of the Artemis II mission so far.After undergoing medical examination, the crew is spending the night (as it is nighttime over there in the US) aboard a US Navy amphibious transport vessel.You can scroll down for the highlights of the mission.We're expecting the astronauts to be reunited with their families later today and we'll be back to bring you live updates then - when we also hope to hear from the astronauts themselves.Watch: Mission around the moon was 'a triumph'The Artemis II mission "didn't just return four brave astronauts home," says our science and technology editor Tom Clarke, "it showed others can go back to land, then live, on the moon."You can watch him talk more about the spectacular achievement here:What 10 days of space travel could mean for Artemis astronauts' healthBy Jake Levison, news reporterThe Artemis II crew are now safely back on Earth after conducting a record-breaking mission to the far side of the moon, where they travelled further from their home planet than anyone in history.Humans have been through millions of years of evolution to become perfectly adapted to life on Earth, so spending time in space - with no gravity, no sunlight and different levels of radiation - poses a real challenge physically.So what were the main health concerns space travel presents and how does NASA contend with them?Space radiationAstronauts are exposed to high-energy radiation in space, unlike on Earth, where the atmosphere and planetary magnetic field provide a shield against it.This can lead to DNA damage, increased cancer risk, neurodegenerative effects, cardiovascular issues and immune system dysregulation, experts say.The International Space Station (ISS), where astronauts spend much of their time, is somewhat protected from radiation by Earth's magnetosphere, as it's around 250 miles away.But the further you go into space, the more radiation you get exposed to, says Dr Haig Aintablian, director of space medicine at UCLA."Once you go beyond low Earth orbit, you lose much of the protection of Earth's magnetic field," he tells Sky News, adding radiation is one of the "real challenges" deep space poses.Effects of microgravityFloating around in space may look like a lot of fun, but gravity plays a critical role in regulating bodily functions, and its absence has negative impacts on human health, according to experts."The body is built to live and work in gravity. When that gravity signal is removed, the inner ear has to recalibrate, muscles and bones are used differently, and fluids shift upward toward the head," Dr Aintablian says."That is why we can see changes in balance, strength and, in some cases, vision."You'll have seen the astronauts using specialist exercise equipment during their journey, and that's to contend with the fact that their bodies are not being engaged by the same forces they are used to on Earth.Vitally, they are known to lose bone density, meaning bones get weaker and more brittle.For every month in space, astronauts' weight-bearing bones become roughly 1% less dense if precautions aren't taken, according to NASA.They can also experience muscle atrophy, the wasting or thinning of muscle tissue, during their time in space.Headaches are also widely reported for people in space. A study published in 2024 found 22 out of 24 surveyed astronauts who travelled in space for up to 26 weeks experienced them frequently while away from Earth.Dr Aintablian says other common health concerns include motion sickness, dizziness, cardiovascular conditioning and sleep disruption.Highlights of Artemis II missionHere, Sky News looks back at the highlights of what the Artemis II mission achieved during nearly 10 days in space.Day 1: Blast off NASA's first crewed mission around the moon in more than 50 years took off on 1 April from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This was also the day the crew reported an issue with the toilet. Day 2: Leaving Earth orbitFor the first time since Apollo 17 in 1972, humans departed Earth orbit onboard the Orion capsule. Day 6: Lunar flybyThe Orion crew made history as they surpassed the record set by Apollo 13 in 1970 as the humans who travelled farthest from Earth.Day 7: Mesmerising moon pictures NASA released the first pictures from the lunar flyby, and they were - excuse the pun - otherworldly.Day 10: Astronauts return to EarthFootage showed the Artemis II crew emerging from the Orion capsule after they successfully returned to Earth.'One of them was even dancing': Crew were 'fit and strong' enough to walk without needing wheelchairs, expert saysThe crew of the Artemis II mission were "fit and strong" enough to walk without needing to use wheelchairs after they arrived on the US Navy's recovery ship, professor Catherine Heymans, astronomer royal for Scotland, has told Sky News."One of them was even dancing," she said, explaining that the mission had examined the impact on the human body of going so far away from Earth."They've been looking at the impact of the harsh space environment on the human body," she explained."They've only been up there for 10 days, they've been doing lots of exercise while they've been there, so their muscles haven't experienced a lot of the degradation that happens in the International Space Station."But the reason they wanted to see them walking off like this is because the long-term vision for these Artemis missions [is] to get boots back on the moon."You can watch the full interview here:'For everything to have gone as well as it seems to have done is remarkable'It was a "near-perfect ending" to the mission, Chris Lintott, professor of astrophysics at the University of Oxford, has told Sky News."For everything to have gone as well as it seems to have done is remarkable," he said after Artemis II splashed down in the Pacific Ocean.He said NASA's top line will be that "this went about as well as we could possibly have expected it to".You can watch his full interview here:Smiles and thumbs up as crew arrive on recovery shipPictures show the four members of the Artemis II crew smiling and giving thumbs up as they arrive on the US Navy's recovery ship John P Murtha.Where are the astronauts now?After the Artemis II crew safely splashed down in the Pacific Ocean following nearly 10 days in space, they were hoisted from the capsule one by one to helicopters hovering overhead.The team were then flown a short distance to a nearby US Navy amphibious transport vessel, the John P Murtha, for further medical examination.They are expected to spend the night aboard the ship and will be flown to Houston on Saturday, where they will be reunited with their families, NASA said.From Star Wars to the moon: Orion programme manager reveals his journeyOne of the team behind the successful return of the Artemis astronauts told the press conference about how his own cosmic journey began - at a screening of Star Wars.Orion programme manager Howard Hu said: "I shared a moment with my father, he took me to see Star Wars. "He's not alive today. I wish he was, because that little kid... was inspired by the stars. And now we're able to send our crew out to the stars. The farthest any humans have been. "I mean, I can't even express just how I feel and the goosebumps I have."And I would say that for all the kids out there... just pursue the dreams."
